title: Purity, Repayment, and a Jealousy Test
overview: This chapter gives three sets of rules for life in Israel's camp: who must stay outside it, how to make amends for wronging someone, and a ritual for a wife whose husband suspects her of adultery.

parts.label: Keeping the camp clean (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: People with certain skin diseases, bodily discharges, or recent contact with a dead body had to stay outside the camp until they were made ritually clean again. The reason given is that God lived among them, so the camp had to be kept fit for his presence; this was about ritual purity, not a judgment on the person's character.

parts.label: Making things right (vv. 5-8)
parts.note: Wronging another person is treated as being unfaithful to God too, so the wrongdoer must admit it, repay the full amount, and add a fifth (20 percent) more. If the injured person had died with no close relative to receive it, the repayment went to the priest, along with a ram offered as a sacrifice to restore the wrongdoer's standing with God.

parts.label: Gifts to priests (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: Anything given to a priest became his to keep, and the giver could not take it back later. People could do as they wished with their own holy gifts until they handed them over.

parts.label: A husband's suspicion (vv. 11-15)
parts.note: This covers a case with no witnesses, where a husband suspects adultery whether or not his wife is actually guilty. He brings her to the priest with a plain barley offering, with no oil or incense, which normally signaled joy and acceptance, because the occasion was grim.

parts.label: The bitter water ritual (vv. 16-28)
parts.note: The priest mixed holy water with dust from the sanctuary floor, loosened the woman's hair, had her accept a curse with "Amen," washed the written curse into the water, and made her drink it. If she was guilty, her body would be harmed in a way linked to childbearing; the Hebrew is unclear, and scholars debate whether it means miscarriage, infertility, or something else.

parts.label: The rule summed up (vv. 29-31)
parts.note: The husband is declared free of blame even if his suspicion was false, and there is no matching rite for a wife who suspects her husband. Some interpreters think the ritual protected women by leaving the verdict to God rather than an angry husband, since the water itself was harmless, while others see it mainly as a sign of how unequal marriage was; later Jewish teachers ended the practice.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to read the jealousy ritual, some seeing it as God limiting a harsh ancient custom to protect accused wives and others seeing it as reflecting the unequal treatment of women in that culture.
think: When someone suspects you of something you cannot disprove, what would a fair way of settling it look like?
